clusters.text: Texas state Senator Angela Paxton says in a new PAC ad that she is voting for the Republican ticket on November 3.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim is accurate as worded. The Texas Tribune, CNN, NBC News and Fox News all report that State Sen. Angela Paxton appears in a Texas PAC ad released Oct. 3, 2026. 
In the ad she says, "That's why I'm voting for the Republican ticket on Nov. 3."
 The Texas Tribune and NBC report that 
Texas PAC is a super PAC affiliated with Senate GOP leadership
, and that she 
did not name Ken Paxton's Senate bid
. The claim says only that she is voting for the Republican ticket, and it doesn't say she named her husband, so that omission doesn't make it misleading. The ad has nothing to do with the election-integrity themes in the context note.

clusters.text: Angela Paxton is the estranged wife of Ken Paxton.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Angela Paxton filed for divorce from Ken Paxton in July 2025. 
The filing says the couple stopped living together "on or about June 1, 2024."
 The case is still pending. 
Time reported that a spokesperson for Angela Paxton said the divorce proceedings are still underway.
 
The scheduled divorce trial was canceled
 in June 2026 as the two sides worked toward a settlement, and I found no report of a final decree. Established outlets use the same word as the claim. 
The Texas Tribune, via KERA, calls Ken Paxton her "estranged husband"
, 
Newsweek calls her his "estranged wife"
, and 
CNN uses "estranged wife" and says she "is divorcing" him.
 One Houston Chronicle piece describes her as "now divorced". That conflicts with Time, Newsweek and CNN, and nothing I found shows a finalized divorce. The claim has nothing to do with election administration, but as worded it is accurate.

clusters.text: Donald Trump met with Tina Peters to discuss an election plan.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The meeting claim traces to Ed Martin, a former DOJ official. 
He said on Real America's Voice on Oct. 5 that Peters had been in the Oval Office about two hours earlier "talking about this question." The reporting describes this as election integrity and plans for upcoming elections.
 Colorado Newsline reports that 
an unnamed source confirmed to ABC News that Peters and Trump met Monday
. However, 
the White House says it does "not comment on private meetings that may or may not have happened,"
 and 
the nature of the plans Peters and Trump discussed is unclear
. Peters's lawyer Peter Ticktin described a ballot-seizure and hand-recount plan, but 
he told Mediaite he did not attend the "last meeting" between Peters and Trump
, so his account is not firsthand. The claim states as fact that Trump discussed "an election plan" with Peters. I found no on-record confirmation from Trump, Peters or the White House, and no primary record of the meeting. The outlets I found rest on Martin's secondhand account and one anonymous source.

clusters.text: Tina Peters met with or was consulted by Trump about a plan to seize ballots nationwide for the midterms.
clusters.verdict_basis:
A meeting is reported but not officially confirmed. Ed Martin, a former DOJ official, said on Real America's Voice on Oct. 5 that Peters was in the Oval Office with Trump "on election integrity". 
The White House said it does not comment on private meetings that may or may not have happened, and an unnamed source confirmed the Monday meeting to ABC News.
 The ballot-seizure part comes only from Peters' lawyer, Peter Ticktin, speaking on Joe Oltmann's podcast. 
He described a plan to take control of ballots right after the machines count them and then recount.
 Colorado Newsline notes that 
the nature of the plans Peters and Trump discussed is unclear.
 Neither Martin nor the White House said the meeting covered a nationwide ballot seizure. No document shows that Trump was consulted on, adopted or endorsed that plan. Several outlets, such as TNR, state more firmly that the meeting "concerned" the plan, but they are relying on Ticktin's account. Ticktin also reportedly cited privilege and limited what he would say. The claim is therefore partly supported: a meeting with Trump is credibly reported. The link to a nationwide ballot-seizure plan is one side's characterization and is unco

clusters.text: Donald Trump suggested Iran could take out Los Angeles and San Diego.
clusters.verdict_basis: ABC News, CNN and ABC7 report that at an Oct. 5, 2026 rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, Trump said Iran "can take out a city" and then "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego." The claim says Trump "suggested" this, and ABC News and CNN use that same verb. The White House (Steven Cheung) and FactCheck.org argue the remarks were a confusingly worded point that a nuclear Iran would have threatened US cities. That dispute is about what Trump meant. It doesn't change that he said the words and the claim doesn't say he advocated an attack. The Hill reports he repeated a similar line at a San Antonio rally, saying "Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles."

clusters.text: A Trump martial law scheme to steal the midterms has leaked and been exposed.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The reporting does not show a leaked Trump scheme. Axios (Oct. 16) reported that MAGA election activists with access to Trump, including his childhood friend Peter Ticktin, are 
pushing for Trump to resort to extraordinary measures, including martial law, if they believe the midterms are "rigged."
 The remarks came on a Sept. 30 activist call streamed on Rumble. Axios also noted 
there is no evidence the elections will be rigged and some proposals go far beyond Trump's legal authority
. The Atlantic, as summarized by Alternet, reported that people in Trump's orbit expect him to claim a national-security emergency. Those are third-party predictions and advocacy, and Ticktin's own phrasing was 
"Either martial law, or step aside."
 The White House's response, as reported by Newsweek, 
said the administration was "taking decisive action to protect our elections"
. I found no leaked document and no official statement or record showing that Trump or his administration has adopted a martial-law plan. The claim presents allies' public advocacy and speculation as a leaked, exposed Trump scheme to "steal" the election, which the sources don't support.

clusters.text: Elon Musk cheated or rigged the 2024 election for Donald Trump.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim says Musk "cheated or rigged" the election. That is not supported as worded. Fact-checkers at 
PolitiFact found that federal and state election officials rebutted claims that Starlink manipulated the 2024 vote counts
. 
Snopes (rated "Unfounded") notes that federal certification requires voting systems to be air-gapped from other networks.
 
CISA said it had no evidence of malicious activity that materially affected election infrastructure.
 The one court record about Musk's conduct is separate from vote tampering. 
His lawyers conceded that the $1 million giveaway winners were "not chosen by chance."
 The giveaway cases were civil fraud suits by petition signers. 
They were settled without any finding of liability.
 I found no court finding or official report that Musk altered votes or the result. His roughly $290 million in spending (
Inquirer
) was disclosed political spending, not evidence of rigging. The claim's word "cheated" is vague, but as most readers would take it, it implies election fraud. The records don't support that.

clusters.text: Donald Trump cheated in the 2024 election.
clusters.verdict_basis:
I found no court ruling, official audit or certification finding that Trump or his campaign cheated in 2024. The Washington Post reported that 
Trump and his allies produced no evidence of widespread voter fraud or attempts to rig this election
. A PBS NewsHour/PolitiFact piece and Al Jazeera's reporting say the same about fraud claims generally: 
researchers have found no evidence of widespread fraud
. The one live legal challenge I found is the Rockland County, New York suit. It alleges vote-count discrepancies, and 
Congress has certified the results declaring Trump the winner, so it won't change the outcome
. Newsweek reports that suit only alleges discrepancies. It does not allege that Trump cheated. Factually.co (an aggregator, not a primary source) summarises the record as showing no credible evidence of cheating. The claim is stated as fact, and I found no primary record that supports it.

clusters.text: Maricopa County sent out thousands of ballots before early voting began, and it was not an error.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The first half is accurate. 
The Maricopa County Recorder's Office said 3,126 ballots were erroneously sent to the Postal Service on Oct. 1, nearly a week ahead of schedule.
 
Early voting and the regular ballot mailing in Arizona both begin on Oct. 7.
 The second half, "it was not an error," is contradicted by every source I found, including the Republican Recorder, Justin Heap. 
Heap said his office did not authorize the early mailing and learned of it only after it happened.
 
Runbeck's CEO said the county was not at fault and called it "pure accident, just a human error."
 
After consulting the County Attorney's Office, Heap said the ballots remain valid and need not be voided or reissued.
 The claim echoes Trump's Oct. 5 remarks. 
He said "Maricopa sent out thousands of ballots illegally, and they got caught, and now they're saying it was an error."
 I found no record, court filing or official finding showing the mailing was deliberate or illegal, so that part is an assertion without evidence. The claim also says the county sent the ballots, but reporting attributes the mailing to the vendor, Runbeck. Maricopa County is in Arizona, not Texas.

clusters.text: ICE has been caught targeting voter registration organizations.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Internal HSI records were released through a Democracy Forward FOIA lawsuit on Oct. 7, 2026. 
CNN reported that DHS's election-fraud operation scrutinized dozens of nonprofit voter-registration groups and considered deploying undercover agents against organizations suspected of helping noncitizens register.
 
Democracy Docket reported that HSI identified the groups using nonprofit search engines, then looked for "derogatory information" on them in other databases.
 
The groups were mainly in Ohio and Pennsylvania, plus New Jersey, D.C. and Minnesota, and the records don't show that any undercover operation went ahead.
 
A DHS spokesperson didn't dispute this. The spokesperson said HSI is "actively rooting out and investigating election fraud wherever it can be found."


The claim is accurate as worded: ICE's investigative arm did investigate voter registration organizations, and the evidence is documentary. Two caveats apply. The documents show investigation and planning, not confirmed undercover action. The reporting I found names no Texas registration groups. The Texas link is that 
ICE listed Texas among its priority states for voter records.

clusters.verdict_basis:

It assumes each county is a 50/50 coin flip and gives a 3% chance per state of landing within recount range. Its own figures are about "1 in 1 octillion" for the counties alone, and a copy of the post gives a combined "1 in 15 undecillion". Neither matches "50 octillion". The premises are also shaky. U.S. News counted 
at least 78 counties flipped from Biden to Trump

. Arizona alone was 
about 5.5%

, so the states were not all "just above" recount thresholds. A Votebeat/Spotlight PA report on the related statistical "fraud" models found that

clusters.text: Donald Trump consulted his lawyer Peter Ticktin about starting a civil war to stop the midterm election.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Reporting does show Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and boyhood friend of Trump, talking about civil war. He told podcaster Joe Oltmann that 
if there is a civil war of any sort, it would be better as martial law with "our side in control of the armaments."
 That was reported by The New Republic and others. The context was a hypothetical in which Democrats win enough seats to remove Trump. 
Ticktin said his client Tina Peters proposed that Trump seize ballots nationwide and hand-recount them
. CNN reported that 
Ticktin joined Peters in the Oval Office for a meeting with Trump
, though a White House official downplayed his relationship with Trump. None of the sources I found shows Trump consulting Ticktin about starting a civil war or stopping the election. The civil-war language is Ticktin's own, said in a hypothetical, and he has also 
denied advocating martial law to operate elections
. The claim therefore overstates the record by attributing Ticktin's comments to Trump and presenting them as a consultation to start a war.

The Time transcript and the other reports contradict that attribution. Martial law talk in this context comes from Trump allies such as Peter Ticktin, not from Trump's Time answers. clusters.text: Trump declined in a Time interview to rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act around the midterms.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Time asked Trump whether he would rule out declaring a state of emergency before the midterms unless there was widespread violence. 
He answered, "I don't rule anything out or in."
 
When Time clarified it meant the Insurrection Act, he said he had never used it but "could use it."
 
NewsNation reported he had not ruled out invoking the Act or declaring a national emergency around the November midterms.
 
MS NOW noted he did not say he would invoke it.
 The claim doesn't say he would, so it is accurate. I did not retrieve Time's own transcript. The wording and the Sept. 28 interview date come from secondary outlets that agree with each other. One outlet (MEAWW) wrongly called Oct. 1 a Monday, which doesn't affect the claim.

clusters.text: Polls show Donald Trump is not doing well ahead of the midterms.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Polling released in October 2026 matches the claim. The NBC News Decision Desk poll (Oct. 18) 
put Trump's approval at 34% among U.S. adults, a second-term low, with disapproval at 66%
. In the same poll, 
registered voters preferred Democrats to control Congress by 55%-45%
. The Silver Bulletin average 
hit an all-time low of net -23.9 over the weekend
 and then 
recovered slightly to -22.3
. A few individual polls are less bad for him, such as TIPP and Noble at about net -13 and -12. Generic-ballot polling also favors Democrats, with an average of about 
Democrats 49.4% to Republicans 41.9%
. The claim is broad but accurate as worded. It makes no specific number, date or attribution that could be wrong.

clusters.text: Polls show fewer Democrats plan to vote by mail in this midterm.
clusters.verdict_basis:
An NBC News poll of 1,000 registered voters, fielded Sept. 11–15, found that 
23% of registered Democrats intend to vote by mail in the midterms, down from 34% in 2024
. Axios and The Hill reported the same figures, and the poll's margin of error is 
plus or minus 3.1 points
. A separate NPR/PBS/Marist poll (Sept. 14–15) put Democrats' mail-voting intent at 32%. That poll said the overall share planning to vote by mail is 
little changed from 2024
, and it doesn't directly compare Democrats with 2024. So the claim is accurate for the NBC poll, which is the one that measured the change. The wording "polls show" (plural) slightly overstates the evidence, and the finding is national rather than specific to Texas.

clusters.text: The Houston Chronicle Editorial Board has endorsed in every key Texas race on November 3.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The Houston Chronicle's November voter guide says 
the Editorial Board endorses in every key race in Texas' Nov. 3 election: Senate, governor, Harris County judge and more.

James Talarico

clusters.text: A new version of chaos is coming that would be used to force martial law and cancel the election.
Nearly one in five registered voters in Tulare, California received two mail-in ballots for the same election.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Tulare County's Registrar of Voters, Michelle Baldwin, said that 
7,791 voters within the county, and more specifically the City of Tulare, received the duplicate ballots
. ABC30 reported that 
all of them went to residents of the city of Tulare, which has more than 34,000 registered voters
. That works out to roughly 23% of the city's registered voters, or nearly one in four. This is more than one in five, so "nearly one in five" understates the share. It also isn't the figure officials gave: they put it at 0.03%, which doesn't match their own counts, since 7,791 of 227,000 county voters is about 3.4%. The core event is real: 
a vendor error during the ballot replacement procedure
 caused it. Officials said 
only a single ballot would be counted and any additional ballots would be rejected
. The claim gives the proportion imprecisely and leaves out the cause and safeguards, and the X post in question presents the incident as evidence of a "cheat". The exact share depends on the city's current registration count, which I did not find. The event occurred, but the number is wrong as worded and the framing is incomplete.

clusters.text: Mass mail-in voting creates messes like the duplicate ballots in Tulare, as Donald Trump has said.

clusters.text: Donald Trump will claim the midterms were rigged if he loses them.
A University of Houston poll of Harris County finds James Talarico leading Ken Paxton 58 to 36.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The University of Houston's Hobby School published the poll. It surveyed 2,750 likely Harris County voters between Oct. 3 and 8, 2026. 
It found Talarico at 58% and Paxton at 36%, with 2% for Libertarian Ted Brown and 4% unsure.

58% to 36%
). The claim says "Harris County", which matches the poll's population. The poll covers likely voters in that county, not the whole state. Co-author Mark Jones said that 
extrapolating the county results statewide would put Talarico ahead by only about one to three points

clusters.text: There is no evidence that the midterm elections are or will be rigged.
clusters.verdict_basis:

A Democracy Forward report says election officials, law enforcement, audits, Congress and the courts have found no evidence of widespread fraud. That group is an advocacy organisation, so I treat it as a secondary source. A Rolling Out piece from Oct. 16 about martial-law demands says 
there is no evidence that the elections will be rigged
. The tracker riggingelections.com cites an NBC News review that found 
the DOJ still cannot substantiate Trump's claims of widespread voter fraud
. I did not open that NBC review myself.

more than 11 million Texans voted in November 2024, so seven is a tiny fraction
. The Secretary of State referred 117 further cases and 
confirmed that 578 other flagged voters are U.S. citizens
. NBC News reported that 
three people had been prosecuted
 as of Aug. 17 under Paxton's noncitizen-voting probe. The DPS failure to process 
over 500,000 voter registrations
 was attributed to

clusters.text: Donald Trump may consider declaring martial law around the midterms.
Elon Musk is deciding the results of American elections.
clusters.verdict_basis:
Reuters and Al Jazeera, citing New York Times reporting and campaign finance records, say 
Musk has spent roughly $366 million this cycle, $276 million of it since July, to help Republicans keep control of Congress
. That likely makes him 
the single biggest political donor in this year's races
. That is real influence over campaigns, but it is spending, not control of results. Voters haven't yet voted in the November 2026 midterms, and PBS/AP reported that Musk-backed groups 
spent over $21 million on the April 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court race, which their candidate lost by 10 points
, so money alone doesn't decide outcomes. Snopes found 
no evidence that Musk rigged the 2024 election through Starlink
 and noted that most election systems are closed networks. I found no reporting or records showing Musk controls vote counting or certification, in Texas or elsewhere. The claim exaggerates his documented donor influence into deciding results.

clusters.text: Federal judges are telling Trump they will approve lawsuits against him if he declares martial law after the midterms.
clusters.verdict_basis:
I found no record or credible reporting of federal judges telling Trump anything about martial law or lawsuits. A MEAWW fact-check of a closely related viral X post, which said dozens of judges were pledging to rule against Trump if he tried to rig the midterms or declare martial law, 
found no public reports, statements, announcements or press conference records of any such pledge
. It also said the post
